brief.outcome: Today, make both leaked credentials (a Stripe secret key and an AWS access key, pushed to a public GitHub repo two days ago) useless to anyone else, find out from the logs whether either was used by someone other than us, and clean up the exposure, with the CTO approving every key rotation and every history rewrite.

ambition.goal_beyond: No secret can reach the repository again, and if one ever does the team finds out and shuts it in minutes, not days.
rungs: Rotate both keys today and report whether the logs show any misuse
Establish what each key could reach, prove from the logs what it actually did (and say honestly where logging cannot tell), close any footholds, and clean the repository and its copies
Keep it true without being asked: push protection and secret scanning on, a pre-commit check, and keys that expire, so the next slip is blocked or caught at once
ambition.judge: AWS CloudTrail and IAM, Stripe request logs and events, and GitHub's own secret scanning alerts and push protection, each an independent record of what the keys did and whether any secret remains; the settings changes are offered at the decision and need the CTO's yes

brief.deliverable: Both credentials rotated and the old ones dead, a sourced misuse finding for AWS and Stripe that says what the logs can and cannot show, the repository history cleaned if the CTO approves, and prevention proposed for the CTO to accept. Notes kept in the repo's private ops folder with no secret values in them.
done: Evidence from AWS and Stripe logs exported before anything is changed
Both leaked credentials rotated and the old ones shown dead, with production health checked
A finding for each key: abused, no evidence of abuse within the logged coverage, or unknown, with the evidence
Any foothold an intruder created (new users, keys, roles, payouts, webhooks) found and closed or confirmed absent
Repository history cleaned and collaborators told, if the CTO approves; forks and cached views dealt with or listed
Prevention proposed and, if the CTO says yes, switched on
Notes saved in the private ops folder with no secrets in them
brief.deadline: Close off today; the abuse finding and cleanup follow the same day or the next
guardrails: No key rotation or history rewrite happens without the CTO's approval of that exact action
Production payments and AWS workloads that use these keys keep working, or any outage is announced to the CTO before it happens
Log evidence is exported and kept before any key is deleted or changed
No secret value is written to notes, chat, pull requests or logs; keys are named by ID or last four characters only
limits: Notes stay in the repo's private ops folder
Key rotation and history rewrite need the CTO's approval each time
Changes in AWS and Stripe are made through the consoles with the CTO's approval; we never hold or paste secret keys
assets: The public GitHub repository and its history
brief.data_home: The repo's private ops folder (the owner said to keep notes there)
brief.technical_level: Not stated by the owner. Give exact steps and ready commands, with plain notes, for the CTO to approve.
unknowns: Whether the keys were used by anyone else (the owner's stated unknown)
The exact time of the push, and when the first copy could have been taken
What permissions the AWS key had and whether it is a root or IAM user key
Whether the Stripe key is live or test mode, and whether it is a restricted key
Which services, deployments and CI jobs use these keys
Whether CloudTrail has a trail beyond the 90-day event history, and whether data events are logged

answers.question: What happened?
answers.answer: A developer pushed a commit to the public GitHub repo two days ago containing a Stripe secret key and an AWS access key in a config file; it was deleted in a later commit but is still in the history

answers.question: What access do we have?
answers.answer: GitHub MCP with admin access; AWS console and Stripe dashboard through the browser

answers.question: What needs approval?
answers.answer: Any key rotation or history rewrite needs the CTO's approval

answers.question: What do you want?
answers.answer: To know if anything was abused and to close it off today

answers.question: Where do notes go?
answers.answer: In the repo's private ops folder

answers.question: What is unknown?
answers.answer: Whether the keys were used by anyone else

research.approach: Practitioners treat any key that touched a public repository as compromised from the moment of the push, because public repositories are scanned continuously: the response is containment first, evidence second, cleanup third. They record what the credential could reach, export the provider logs before changing anything, then disable (not delete) the AWS key and roll the Stripe key, restore service with new credentials from a secrets store, and only then read the logs for misuse and for footholds such as new IAM users, keys, payout destinations or webhooks. Rewriting git history is a cleanup step, not a fix: it cannot recall copies in clones, forks and caches, so rotation is what actually closes the exposure. Logs have limits (CloudTrail event history shows 90 days of management events only), so a clean log is reported as no evidence of abuse within what was logged, never as proof of none.

sources.title: Manage access keys for IAM users (AWS IAM User Guide)
sources.note: Access keys are long-term credentials; keep them out of project files; use CloudTrail to monitor key usage; two keys per user, so a new key can be created before the old one is removed. Page shows no date; accessed 2026-11-03.

sources.title: Working with CloudTrail event history (AWS CloudTrail User Guide)
sources.note: Event history is a searchable, downloadable record of the past 90 days of management events, per Region, one attribute filter at a time; it does not show data events; a trail or event data store is needed for longer or wider coverage. Page shows no date; accessed 2026-11-03.

sources.title: Protecting against compromised API keys (Stripe Support)
sources.note: Roll the key now, update the backend, delete the old key once the new one works, review connected accounts, payouts and bank accounts, reverse unauthorized payouts, refund fraudulent charges, audit usage, rotate other keys. Page shows no date; accessed 2026-11-03.

sources.title: Best practices for managing secret API keys (Stripe Docs)
sources.note: Treat any exposure as a potential compromise and rotate even if unsure anyone saw it; keep keys in a secrets vault; use restricted keys; audit request logs; Stripe may notify or deactivate exposed keys but does not guarantee detection. Page shows no date; accessed 2026-11-03.

sources.title: Removing sensitive data from a repository (GitHub Docs)
sources.note: Rotate or revoke first; rewriting history cannot clean clones and forks, changes commit hashes, hides closed pull request diffs; GitHub Support can remove cached views only for data rotation cannot mitigate; git-filter-repo with --sensitive-data-removal. Page shows no date; accessed 2026-11-03.

sources.title: About push protection (GitHub Docs)
sources.note: Blocks pushes with secrets before they land; repository-level protection is off by default and an admin must enable it; bypasses create alerts and audit entries. Page shows no date; accessed 2026-11-03.

steps.name: Record what leaked, since when, where copies may be, and where each key is used
steps.why: Scope decides everything: which keys, how long exposed, what can reach them, and which services will break when they are rotated.

steps.name: Export provider logs before changing anything
steps.why: CloudTrail event history is limited to 90 days and Stripe logs are the only record of what the key did; evidence is kept before keys are changed.

steps.name: Check what the logs can and cannot prove
steps.why: Event history has no data events and covers one Region at a time, so absence of misuse needs a stated coverage.

steps.name: Rotate both keys and kill the old ones
steps.why: Rotation, not history rewriting, closes the exposure; AWS key disabled first and deleted later, Stripe key rolled and replaced in the backend.

steps.name: Read the logs for misuse and footholds
steps.why: Intruders use a leaked key to create new access (users, keys, roles, payout destinations, webhooks), which survives rotation.

steps.name: Clean the repository, copies and cached views
steps.why: History rewrite removes the file from the default history but not from forks, clones or cached views; GitHub Support handles cached views.

steps.name: Block the next leak
steps.why: Push protection and a vault stop secrets reaching the repo; short-lived or restricted keys limit the damage of a slip.

steps.name: Verify the old keys are dead and nothing new was used
steps.why: Closing is proven by the provider consoles and logs, not by the plan.

steps.name: Write a blameless note and propose lasting rules

pitfalls.text: Rewriting history first and rotating later, or treating the rewrite as the fix, while the key stays valid and copies remain in forks and clones.
Deleting the AWS key before exporting logs and recording what it could reach.
Reading a quiet log as proof of no misuse when event history shows only 90 days of management events in one Region at a time.
Rotating the Stripe key but not updating the backend, which takes payments down, or leaving the old key alive on a long expiry.
Missing footholds that survive rotation: new IAM users or keys, changed roles, new payout accounts or webhook endpoints.
Writing the secret into notes, tickets or chat while documenting the incident.

plan.name: Close off the leaked keys today and prove what they did

capabilities.name: Read repository history, forks, traffic and alerts (GitHub MCP)
capabilities.why: Find the commit, its time, forks, clones and secret scanning alerts.

capabilities.name: Read IAM, CloudTrail and billing (AWS console, browser)
capabilities.why: Key permissions, last used, event history and spend.

capabilities.name: Read request logs, events, payouts and settings (Stripe dashboard, browser)
capabilities.why: See what the key did and what was changed.

capabilities.name: Disable and replace the AWS access key (CTO, AWS console)
capabilities.why: The CTO approves and makes each change; we never hold the secret.

capabilities.name: Roll the Stripe secret key (CTO, Stripe dashboard)
capabilities.why: The CTO approves and makes each change; the new key goes straight to the secrets store.

capabilities.name: Rewrite history and change repository security settings (GitHub MCP, admin)
capabilities.why: Force-push a cleaned history and switch on push protection, each only after the CTO's yes.

data.name: Repository facts
data.why: Which commit, when, who saw it, and where else it may be.

routes.how: GitHub MCP: commit, repository forks, traffic and secret scanning alerts.

data.name: Where the keys are used
data.why: Rotating breaks whatever still uses the old key.

routes.how: Search the repository, workflow files and deploy config for the key IDs and variable names.
Ask the CTO which other systems or people hold copies.

data.name: AWS activity for the key
data.why: What the key did, from where, in which Regions.

routes.how: CloudTrail Event history, filtered by the access key ID, each Region in use plus all others, last 90 days, downloaded as files; or the CLI lookup-events command.
Ask whether a trail or event data store exists for longer coverage and data events.

data.alternative: If only the console view can be read, findings are limited to what is on screen and marked low confidence.

data.name: AWS account state
data.why: Footholds and spend: users, keys, roles, policies, running resources.
fields: IAM users and keys with last used
policies attached to the leaked identity

routes.how: IAM credential report; resource and cost views by Region in the console.

data.name: Stripe activity for the key
data.why: What the key did, from where.

routes.how: Stripe Workbench or Developers, request logs filtered to the key, last 90 days where available.

data.name: Stripe account state
data.why: Footholds and money movement: payouts, bank accounts, webhooks, connected accounts, team.

routes.how: Dashboard lists exported or read for the period since the push.

stages.name: Pin down the incident
stages.goal: Turn the owner's words into a scoped incident, limits and the access we have. Writes BRIEF.md. No secret value is recorded.

stages.name: Scope the exposure
stages.goal: From the repository, record which commit leaked which keys (by ID or last four only), the time of the push, forks and clone traffic, secret scanning alerts, any other secrets in the history, and every place the keys are used.

checks.name: No file in the engagement folder contains a full key; a search for the key patterns returns nothing
Push time, first-seen time and detection time are stated with sources; the exposure window in hours is computed
All branches, tags and pull request refs were scanned for other secrets, and the count found (including zero) is stated
Every service, CI job and person that uses the old keys is listed, so rotation does not surprise production

stages.name: Export the provider logs now
stages.goal: Before any key changes, export AWS CloudTrail event history for the key in every Region, the IAM credential report, and Stripe request logs, payouts, bank accounts, webhooks and team, into the ops folder.

outputs.name: What was exported and its limits

checks.name: The export time is earlier than any key change, shown by timestamps
Every AWS Region was searched for the access key ID, or the skipped Regions are listed
The export covers from before the push time to now, or the shortfall is stated
Exports contain key IDs only, never secret values

stages.name: Check what the logs can prove
stages.goal: State what the logging covers and does not: event history length, Regions, management versus data events, trail or event data store, Stripe log retention, so a quiet log is read correctly.

checks.name: Each log source states its first and last event time and what event types it does not record
Any gap between the push time and the first available event is listed
Ends with CHECKED, LIMITED or UNRELIABLE for AWS and for Stripe, and what that means for a no-abuse finding

stages.name: CTO chooses the response
stages.goal: The CTO approves rotating both keys now, and chooses whether to rewrite history, how to tell collaborators and whether to accept the prevention settings. Each is a separate yes or no.

checks.name: Rotation, history rewrite, collaborator notice and prevention settings are each a separate recorded decision with the CTO's reason
For each choice, what could break (which service uses the key, who must re-clone) and the rollback are stated

stages.name: Rotate both keys and kill the old ones
stages.goal: With the CTO approving each action: create the replacement AWS key and put it in the secrets store, deploy, then deactivate (not delete) the old AWS key; roll the Stripe key, update the backend, confirm payments, and expire the old key. Read each result back.

checks.name: Each rotation step has the CTO's approval recorded first
The AWS console shows the old key Inactive and the Stripe dashboard shows the old key expired, read back after the change
A production payment and a representative AWS-backed request succeed on the new keys after the change
No new key value appears in any note, chat or log; it goes straight to the secrets store
The AWS key is deleted only after the logs are exported and the abuse finding is written

stages.name: Read the logs for misuse
stages.goal: Test the hypotheses against the exported logs and state, separately for AWS and Stripe, whether there is evidence of misuse and of footholds, and what the logs cannot show.

checks.name: Every listed hypothesis is SUPPORTED, REFUTED or UNKNOWN with the log lines or counts behind it
Source IPs and user agents are compared with the team's known list; unknown ones are listed with their first and last time
Activity is split into before and after the push time
New IAM users, keys, roles, policies, payout destinations, bank accounts and webhooks since the push are listed or confirmed absent
The finding uses ABUSE FOUND, NO EVIDENCE OF ABUSE WITHIN LOGGED COVERAGE, or UNKNOWN, never 'safe' without coverage

stages.name: Clean the repository and block the next leak
stages.goal: With the CTO approving each action: rewrite history to remove the file (if chosen), tell collaborators to re-clone, list forks and ask for cached views to be removed, and switch on push protection and secret scanning (if chosen).

checks.name: History is rewritten only after both keys are shown dead, and the CTO's approval is recorded
After the rewrite a search of every branch, tag and ref finds no key pattern, or the remaining refs are listed
Forks and clones are listed with what was done about each, and cached views are requested through GitHub Support where needed
Push protection and secret scanning status is read back from the repository settings

stages.name: Prove it is closed
stages.goal: Read the consoles and logs to show both old keys are dead, no new attempts succeed, and no open secret scanning alert remains, then watch for 7 days for any use of the old keys.

checks.name: Both old credentials read as dead in the provider consoles on the day and again after 7 days
Any attempts with the old keys after rotation are listed (AWS access denied events, Stripe failed requests) with source IPs, or confirmed none
Open secret scanning alerts for the repository are zero, or each is explained
Metric reads 0 credentials valid only if both are shown dead; the abuse finding is restated with its coverage

stages.name: Keep what we learned
stages.goal: Write a blameless timeline, a runbook for the next leak and the prevention rules proposed to the CTO.

checks.name: A sourced timeline from the push to closure, with times
The note contains no secret values and no private customer data
Each proposed rule (vault, expiring or restricted keys, pre-commit scan, who can push to the public repo) says its scope and owner, and nothing is switched on without the CTO's yes

hypotheses.statement: Someone other than us used the AWS key.
hypotheses.test: CloudTrail events for the access key ID in every Region since the push time, by source IP and user agent.
hypotheses.confirm_if: Any event from an IP or user agent not on the team's known list, after the push time.
hypotheses.refute_if: All events are from known sources or there are none, and the log coverage verdict is CHECKED.

hypotheses.statement: An intruder created access that survives rotation.
hypotheses.test: Events creating or changing IAM users, access keys, login profiles, roles, trust policies or policies since the push time.
hypotheses.confirm_if: Any such event not made by the team.
hypotheses.refute_if: None found and the IAM credential report shows no unknown users or keys.

hypotheses.statement: Resources were launched or spend rose.
hypotheses.test: Running resources and cost by Region and service against the prior month.
hypotheses.confirm_if: Resources in a Region the team does not use, or a service with zero prior spend now billed.
hypotheses.refute_if: Resources and cost match the prior pattern.

hypotheses.statement: Data was read or copied with the AWS key.
hypotheses.test: Data event logs, if they exist, for storage, secrets and database snapshots; otherwise the key's permissions.
hypotheses.confirm_if: Read or copy events for data by the key after the push time.
hypotheses.refute_if: Data events exist, cover the period, and show none; otherwise this stays UNKNOWN.

hypotheses.statement: Someone other than us used the Stripe key.
hypotheses.test: Request logs for the key by source IP, endpoint and status since the push time.
hypotheses.confirm_if: Any request from an IP not belonging to our servers, or any list-all or export call we do not make.
hypotheses.refute_if: All requests are from our servers and match our integration's endpoints.

hypotheses.test: Payouts, external accounts, refunds, new customers or charges, and webhook endpoints since the push time.
hypotheses.confirm_if: Any payout or bank account we do not recognise, or a new webhook endpoint.

hypotheses.statement: Other secrets are in the history.
hypotheses.test: Scan all branches, tags and pull request refs with GitHub secret scanning and a local scanner.
hypotheses.confirm_if: One or more other live secrets are found.
hypotheses.refute_if: None found after scanning all refs.

hypotheses.statement: Copies of the history exist outside our control.
hypotheses.test: Fork count, clone traffic and cached views.
hypotheses.confirm_if: Any fork exists, or unknown clones are recorded.
hypotheses.refute_if: No forks and clone traffic matches the team.

measurement.window: Same day for the closure check, then 7 days of watching for any use of the old keys.
measurement.min_volume: Not a sampling question: every log event for the two key IDs from the push time onward is read.
measurement.stop_rule: If any foothold or live misuse is found, stop the cleanup, tell the CTO at once and widen containment before anything else.
